headline: MBTA says 532 seniors enrolled on first day of free-fare pilot
dek: The first-day total gives Massachusetts officials an early measure of demand for free MBTA travel for residents 75 and older who no longer drive, while longer-term ridership remains unknown.
body: The Massachusetts Bay Transportation Authority said 532 people successfully enrolled in its Car-Free Seniors Pilot on Oct. 13, the first day applications were available. The agency announced the figure Oct. 14, and Boston 25 News reported Thursday that more than 500 people had enrolled. The number measures completed enrollments, not trips taken, and the MBTA has not released a forecast for how many eligible residents may ultimately join.

The pilot gives Massachusetts residents age 75 and older who no longer drive free travel on MBTA buses, subways, ferries and Commuter Rail. That makes the first-day figure an early sign of demand for a program aimed at preserving transportation access after an older resident stops driving. It does not yet show whether participants are using the system regularly, which routes they need or how the program will affect total ridership.

Enrollment requires a Massachusetts identification card issued through the Registry of Motor Vehicles, rather than a driver's license. Residents who do not already have a Mass ID must obtain one before requesting the free-fare credential. The MBTA and RMV are partners in the program, so the first step is both an eligibility check and a practical access hurdle for people who may not already use state transportation services.

Eligible residents can apply online or in person at the Charlie Service Center at 296 Washington St. in Boston, near the State Street and Downtown Crossing stations. The MBTA says online applicants can receive the credential by mail or choose in-person pickup. Applicants who go to the service center can receive a temporary credential the same day, while a permanent credential is mailed later.

The launch follows a Sept. 23 announcement from Gov. Maura Healey's administration that set Oct. 13 as the opening date. The earlier announcement described the program as part of a broader affordability package that also included half-price monthly Commuter Rail passes from September through November, an expanded $1 Weekend Companion Fare, a wider two-hour transfer window and the removal of higher express-bus fares.

Those policies address different parts of the cost and access problem. The senior pilot is targeted to people who have stopped driving, while the other changes apply to broader groups of riders and different modes. For an older resident in eastern Massachusetts, the value of the new credential will depend not only on the absence of a fare but also on whether bus, rail and ferry schedules connect home with medical appointments, shopping, social activities and family support.

The MBTA and state officials have presented the early enrollment as evidence that the benefit is useful, but the available announcement does not include a geographic breakdown, demographic details, application totals that were not completed or the cost of the pilot. Boston 25 described the rollout as a developing story. Those missing measures will matter as the agency evaluates whether initial interest translates into sustained use and whether the pilot should continue or expand.

For now, the next step for eligible residents is to secure a Massachusetts ID if needed and apply through the MBTA's online process or the Boston service center. The first-day total shows that hundreds acted as soon as enrollment opened; it does not establish the program's long-term reach. The MBTA's Oct. 14 announcement is available at https://www.mbta.com/news, and Boston 25 News' independent report is at https://www.boston25news.com/news/local/more-than-500-seniors-enroll-mbtas-car-free-pilot-program/IKFHRFMSOBHFTGV7U2CNIGY764/.
author: NorthEast News Desk
seoTitle: Free MBTA fares for non-driving seniors open Oct. 13
seoDescription: Massachusetts will open Oct. 13 enrollment for a pilot giving eligible residents 75 and older who no longer drive free MBTA fares.
